newsitem.title: UK: Insurers face more power claims, says US law firm.
newsitem.headline: Insurers face more power claims, says US law firm.

text.p: Insurance and power companies face an increase in litigation over alleged adverse health effects of electro-magnetic fields, despite a lack of scientific proof of cause and effect, U.S. law firm representatives told an insurance seminar on Monday.

"Nobody has been able to prove that electro-magnetic fields cause cancer, but that doesn't mean there isn't a connection...The plaintiff's bar can present a very simple and appealing case," said Dr H.B. Graves, scientific director of U.S. law firm Leboeuf, Lamb, Greene & Macrae (LLG&M).
Litigants have focused their attention in the U.S. and other countries on the possibility that electric power lines, cellular telephones and other appliances may adversely affect people's health.

"We have not been able to demonstrate adverse health effects, but we have not been able to demonstrate that there is not a causative effect," added Graves, who has been involved in electro-magnetic field (EMF) research since the late 1960s.

Graves said the balance of evidence and research indicated there was no danger from EMF, noting that much greater use of electricity in recent decades had not been mirrored by an increase in diseases such as childhood cancer.

Plaintiffs' lawyers looking for scientific evidence of cause and effect had not been able to find the sort of correlation that existed between rising cigarette production and an increase in the incidence of lung cancer, he said.
LLG&M lawyer Russell Yates said plaintiffs' lawyers were concentrating their efforts on certain cases, particularly those involving children and brain tumours.
"These cases aren't going to go away," he said, but added that no cases of personal injury had yet been won where it had been claimed that EMF was the cause of an illness.
